column5: measure, number, weight
column6: The commentary says qaddara assigns each thing its measure and limit; Wisdom says the Creator ordered all things by measure, number and weight, making proportion explicit as the structure of creation.

column5: earth measured by its maker
column6: The commentary glosses qaddara as setting the amount of every thing; Job asks who determined earth's measurements and stretched its line, giving that claim a concrete creation image.

column5: measuring waters and heavens
column6: The commentary reads God's measure as extending across all creation; Isaiah pictures God measuring waters and marking off the heavens, a direct image of cosmic ordering.

column5: appointed times and boundaries
column6: The commentary says measure includes where a thing reaches and when it ends; Acts says God fixed nations' times and habitation boundaries, extending that ordering to human history and geography.

column5: people seek and find God
column6: The commentary joins God's universal measure to guidance; Paul says the bounded times and places are so people will seek God and perhaps find him, giving human purpose to the allotted setting.

column5: numbered days and fixed bounds
column6: The commentary explicitly includes lifespan and endpoint in measure; Job says a person's days are determined and bounds set that cannot be passed, making temporal limit part of created measure.

column5: an appointed season for every matter
column6: The commentary reads grass's greening and withering as one measured course; Ecclesiastes says every matter under heaven has its season, framing change as timed rather than contradictory.

column5: time to plant and uproot, be born and die
column6: The commentary connects pasture's growth and decay with a thing's endpoint; Ecclesiastes sets planting beside uprooting and birth beside death, extending the cycle from vegetation to human life.

column5: life's times held by God
column6: The commentary says every thing has an amount and term; the psalmist says his times are in God's hand, turning the measure of lifespan into personal trust.

column5: moon marks seasons; sun knows its setting
column6: The commentary links measure to cycles that reach an end; the psalm assigns the moon to appointed seasons and the sun to its setting, showing timekeeping within creation.

column5: creatures wait for food in due season
column6: The commentary leaves the object of measuring and guiding unstated so it can cover every being; the psalm says all creatures look to God for food in its season, giving that scope a concrete ecological form.

column5: God opens his hand and satisfies creatures
column6: The commentary leaves the object of measuring and guiding unstated so it can cover every being; the psalm says God gives food, creatures gather it and are satisfied when he opens his hand, specifying how that provision arrives.

column5: breath withdrawn and creatures die
column6: The commentary reads growth and withering as two ends of one measured course; the psalm says God takes away creatures' breath and they die and return to dust, making the endpoint explicit.

column5: breath sent and earth renewed
column6: The commentary reads pasture's withering as one end of a measured course; the psalm says God sends breath and creatures are created and the earth renewed, joining an endpoint to renewed life.

column5: God rejoices in his works
column6: The commentary presents the course of pasture and its end as part of one ordered work; the psalm closes its creation survey with God's rejoicing in his works, adding affirmation to their measured variety.

column5: stars counted and named
column6: The commentary says measure reaches every created thing; the psalm says God counts the stars and calls each by name, combining number with individual address.

column5: rain prepares the earth and grass
column6: The commentary connects measured rain with pasture's emergence; the psalm says God prepares rain and makes grass grow on the hills, directly joining ordered water to vegetation.

column5: God feeds young ravens
column6: The commentary insists that guidance and measure are not limited to humans; the psalm says God gives food even to young ravens that cry, extending providence to vulnerable animals.

column5: starry host brought out by number and name
column6: The commentary says God's measure covers everything; Isaiah says the Creator brings out the host by number and calls each one by name, making universal order both numerical and particular.

column5: sand set as the sea's boundary
column6: The commentary defines measure as also setting a limit; Jeremiah says God set sand as a boundary the sea cannot cross, an image of a created force held within its assigned reach.

column5: rain on uninhabited land
column6: The commentary says the objectless verbs include all beings, not only people; Job asks who sends rain on land where no human lives, placing divine provision beyond human use.

column5: wilderness made to sprout
column6: The commentary links measured rain to pasture's growth; Job says rain makes the desolate ground sprout with grass, showing water, land and vegetation in a specific sequence.

column5: food for ravens and their young
column6: The commentary extends God's guidance beyond humanity; Job asks who provides food for ravens when their young cry to God, making animal dependence part of the Creator's ordering.

column5: hawk's migration by God's wisdom
column6: The commentary says a created being receives a way suited to its nature; God asks Job whether the hawk flies south by Job's wisdom, presenting animal movement as beyond human control and within divine wisdom.

column5: seedtime, harvest and recurring seasons
column6: The commentary reads pasture's green growth and dark decay as stages in one measured course; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will continue, adding covenant assurance to natural cycles.

column5: earth watered and grain prepared
column6: The commentary says rain descends by a measure that supports pasture; the psalm depicts God watering the land and preparing grain, joining measured provision to harvest.

column5: tree bearing fruit in its season
column6: The commentary reads vegetation's growth and withering as a bounded course; the psalm's tree yields fruit in season and keeps its leaf, turning the seasonal image toward the life shaped by Torah.

column5: moon appointed for seasons and signs
column6: The commentary connects the moon's measured phases with time and return; Sirach says the moon serves as a sign of times and seasons, presenting the calendar as part of creation's order.

column5: fixed courses and gates of the sun
column6: The commentary says celestial bodies follow measured courses and mark time; Enoch describes the sun's assigned course through gates, expanding the same motif into an apocalyptic calendar.

column5: heavenly constellation makes each herb grow
column6: The commentary says God's measure and guidance extend to pasture and every creature; Genesis Rabbah interprets creation by saying each herb has a heavenly constellation that prompts its growth, making divine ordering intimate at the level of a plant.

column5: cloud and fire leading Israel
column6: The commentary presents hidaya as a guide going ahead on the route; Exodus says the Lord went before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night to lead them, giving the image a national journey.

column5: Israel travels when the cloud lifts
column6: The commentary says guidance determines both direction and the course's timing; Numbers says Israel camped or set out according to the cloud's movement, making rest and travel part of the guidance.

column5: ark goes ahead to seek a resting place
column6: The commentary describes a guide who leads toward a destination or home; Numbers says the ark traveled ahead for three days to find a resting place, pairing leading with the place sought.

column5: God goes ahead to find a camp
column6: The commentary says the guide moves in front and identifies where the journey should end; Moses recalls God going ahead of Israel to search out a place to camp, by fire at night and cloud by day.

column5: God finds and guards Israel in the wilderness
column6: The commentary develops the image of a guide responsible for a flock; Moses's song recalls God finding Israel in a desert waste, guarding and caring for him, giving the guidance motif a wilderness history.

column5: eagle stirs and carries its young
column6: The commentary links leading with a creature moving ahead and carrying others along; the song compares God's care for Israel to an eagle hovering over its young and bearing them on its pinions.

column5: YHWH alone leads Israel
column6: The commentary says the guide brings the follower along rather than merely pointing from afar; Moses says YHWH alone led Israel and no foreign god was with him, specifying the source and exclusivity of that guidance.

column5: Abram goes to a land God will show
column6: The commentary connects Abraham's confession that his Creator will guide him with a personal journey; Genesis has God tell Abram to go toward a land God will show, making trust in guidance an enacted departure.

column5: servant led by God to the bride
column6: The commentary notes that h-d-y can mean leading a bride to her husband; Abraham's servant blesses God for leading him on the right path to Rebekah for Isaac, combining guidance and the bride's destination in one scene.

column5: YHWH named as the speaker's shepherd
column6: The commentary's flock image presents the guide as caretaker; the psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, making the leader's relation to the follower personal.

column5: shepherd leads to pasture and water
column6: The commentary's flock-and-pasture image presents the guide as caretaker; the psalm's shepherd makes the speaker lie in green pastures and leads him beside waters, joining direction to sustenance.

column5: shepherd leads on right paths
column6: The commentary distinguishes showing a path from the traveler's following it; the psalm says the shepherd leads the speaker on right paths, supplying the route and the ethical quality of the way.

column5: staff and presence in a dark valley
column6: The commentary connects a guide with a staff that reaches the ground before the walker and with shared travel; the psalm says the shepherd remains with the speaker through a dark valley, with rod and staff as comfort.

column5: light and truth lead to God's dwelling
column6: The commentary says a guide shows both the path and the home it reaches; the psalm asks God's light and truth to lead the speaker to the holy mountain and dwelling, joining illumination to destination.

column5: Moses and Aaron lead Israel like a flock
column6: The commentary places a flock's leader between God's sovereignty and pasture; the psalm retells the Exodus as God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, making human guides agents of divine guidance.

column5: lost travelers led to an inhabited city
column6: The commentary says a guide reveals the way and the home at its end; the psalm describes wanderers in a desert waste whom God leads by a straight way to an inhabited city, closely joining route and arrival.

column5: word as lamp for feet and path
column6: The commentary connects a distant light and a guide with a traveler's way; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and a light on the path, making instruction something that illuminates the next steps.

column5: voice says which way to walk
column6: The commentary says guidance is more than pointing at a distant destination and includes a direction for the walk; Isaiah describes a voice behind the people telling them, “This is the way; walk in it,” when they turn aside.

column5: God leads the blind on unknown roads
column6: The commentary says the objectless guidance applies broadly and can bring someone to a way not yet known; Isaiah says God will lead the blind by a way they do not know, turn darkness to light and rough places level.

column5: God teaches and leads in the way to go
column6: The commentary joins the same Lord's act of measuring with his act of guidance; Isaiah calls God Israel's teacher and the one who leads it in the way it should go, an especially close prophetic formulation.

column5: shepherd leads to springs of water
column6: The commentary joins a guide, pasture and provision; Isaiah's restored people are led by the one who has compassion on them and guided beside springs, giving the shepherd-like journey a restoration setting.

column5: continual guidance in dry ground
column6: The commentary relates measured rain and pasture to the path of life; Isaiah says the Lord will guide continually and make the people like a watered garden, bringing guidance and sustained provision together.

column5: God leads Israel beside streams on a straight path
column6: The commentary says guidance reveals both route and destination; Jeremiah depicts Israel returning with weeping and supplication as God leads them beside streams on a straight path, as a father leads Ephraim.

column5: God gathers scattered sheep
column6: The commentary uses a flock's leading to connect care with pasture; Ezekiel says God will bring scattered sheep out from the peoples and gather them from the countries, giving the shepherd image a restoration scene.

column5: God feeds the flock in good pasture
column6: The commentary names pasture as the concrete provision following guidance; Ezekiel says the flock will feed on rich pasture on Israel's mountains, pairing the shepherd's direction with nourishment.

column5: shepherd gives the flock rest
column6: The commentary treats a measured course as including where a creature settles; Ezekiel says God will feed his sheep and make them lie down, adding rest as part of the shepherd's care.

column5: lost, injured and weak sheep restored
column6: The commentary's guide image includes leading and care for the flock; Ezekiel's shepherd seeks the lost, binds the injured and strengthens the weak, specifying what the divine shepherd does for those who cannot proceed unaided.

column5: God teaches Ephraim to walk
column6: The commentary develops a form of walking while leaning on another; Hosea says God taught Ephraim to walk and took him up by the arms, making guidance bodily and accompanied.

column5: guidance by cords of kindness
column6: The commentary says hidaya can be gentle guidance rather than forceful dragging; Hosea describes God drawing Israel with human cords and bands of love, giving that noncoercive relation a specific image.

column5: shepherd with staff among pasture lands
column6: The commentary connects the guide's staff with a flock and its pasture; Micah asks God to shepherd his people with his staff in Bashan and Gilead, making the same image a prayer for restored care.

column5: shepherd calls sheep and leads them out
column6: The commentary says the guide goes ahead and knows the way of the flock; Jesus's shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, making personal recognition part of guidance.

column5: shepherd goes ahead; sheep follow
column6: The commentary distinguishes God's showing from the traveler's following; John says the shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow because they know his voice, directly separating leader's act from follower's response.

column5: one flock and one shepherd
column6: The commentary places the leader of a flock between the guide and pasture; Jesus says other sheep will be brought in so there will be one flock and one shepherd, extending the image to gathered people.

column5: Lamb shepherds and guides to living springs
column6: The commentary joins shepherding, guidance and the arrival at provision; Revelation says the Lamb will shepherd the redeemed and guide them to springs of living water, carrying the pastoral image into final restoration.

column5: angel directs Philip to the Gaza road
column6: The commentary says guidance can set a person on an actual route; an angel tells Philip to go south to the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, making divine direction concrete in a journey.

column5: Spirit directs Philip toward the chariot
column6: The commentary distinguishes the guide's act from the traveler's response; the Spirit tells Philip to approach the chariot, and Philip runs to it, showing guidance received and acted upon.

column5: Spirit guides into all truth
column6: The commentary says hidaya is wider than conversion and means guiding a way; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth, extending guidance to understanding and witness.

column5: Moses turns toward a flame in the wilderness
column6: The commentary recalls Moses seeing a distant fire while seeking help on the road; Exodus says a flame in the bush catches Moses's attention, where the traveler encounters the God who will commission him.

column5: Moses sent to lead Israel out
column6: The commentary says Moses moves from a traveler looking for guidance to a guide sent before Pharaoh; Exodus says God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out, making that change of role a liberation commission.

column5: Wisdom guides Israel on a marvelous way
column6: The commentary presents Moses's account as creation followed by guidance and provision; Wisdom retells the Exodus by saying Wisdom guided the righteous on a marvelous way and sheltered them by day and night, interpreting the journey as Wisdom's work.

column5: Wisdom brings Israel through the sea
column6: The commentary says a guide leads followers toward their destination; Wisdom's Exodus retelling says Wisdom brought Israel through the sea, adding the rescue at the route's decisive obstacle.

column5: food allotted as one's portion
column6: The commentary says qaddara can mean preparing an amount suited to its recipient; Proverbs asks for the food that is one's portion, making measured provision an ethical request for neither excess nor want.

column5: manna gathered by each person's need
column6: The commentary says the measure of a thing prepares it for its use; Moses tells Israel to gather manna according to what each can eat and an omer per person, giving divine provision an explicit daily quantity.

column5: much gathered and little gathered both suffice
column6: The commentary says measured provision is not humiliation but a fit amount; Exodus says the one who gathered much had no excess and the one who gathered little had no lack, showing the provision's measure by its result.

column5: life and death placed before Israel to choose
column6: The commentary says the same shown path may be followed or avoided, without forced movement; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life, giving the human response an explicit covenant form.

column5: human choice between life and death
column6: The commentary says guidance does not drag the traveler and that people may choose the path; Sirach says God made humans and left them to their own choice, then sets fire and water and life and death before them.

column5: all is foreseen, choice is granted
column6: The commentary holds divine guidance together with the person's decision to follow or turn aside; Avot's maxim says all is foreseen yet freedom of choice is given, preserving both claims in a Jewish ethical formulation.

column5: fear of Heaven left to human response
column6: The commentary says showing the road is God's act while taking it is the traveler's; the Talmud says everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven, marking the human response as the point not compelled.

column5: two ways, life and death
column6: The commentary says the shown way divides into people who heed instruction and those who avoid it; the Didache opens with the way of life and the way of death, then gives their different conduct, making the moral fork concrete.

column5: human plans, Lord establishes steps
column6: The commentary warns that a person's own measuring can replace the path God shows; Proverbs says the heart plans its way but the Lord establishes a person's steps, distinguishing intention from the course taken.

column5: no human instructs God's Spirit
column6: The commentary calls it a misjudgment to measure God by human assumptions about revelation; Isaiah asks who directed the Spirit of the Lord or taught him the path of justice, refusing to make human judgment the standard.

column5: God apportions a measure of faith
column6: The commentary warns that people should not replace God's measure with their own; Paul tells each person to think soberly according to the measure of faith God apportioned, applying measure to humility and communal life.

column5: grace given according to Christ's measure
column6: The commentary says measure fits each thing for its purpose; Paul says grace was given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, making differentiated vocation a Christian application of measured provision.

column5: created for works prepared to walk in
column6: The commentary links creation to the way that follows immediately after it; Ephesians says believers are created for good works God prepared beforehand for them to walk in, closely joining making and a prepared path.

column5: Father feeds the birds
column6: The commentary says the objectless measure and guidance encompass every creature; Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor reap yet are fed by the heavenly Father, making nonhuman provision a sign of God's care.

column5: God clothes the grass
column6: The commentary links the measured life of pasture to its growth and decay; Jesus asks disciples to consider how the field's grass grows and is clothed by God, making vegetation an example of provision beyond human effort.

column5: sparrows fall under the Father's care
column6: The commentary says God's measure extends to every being; Jesus says not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father, making even a small creature's fate part of that scope.

column5: hairs counted
column6: The commentary says measure includes particulars rather than only broad cosmic totals; Jesus says the disciples' hairs are all numbered, turning divine measure into individual knowledge.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons and food
column6: The commentary connects measured rain to pasture and sustenance; Paul says God gives rain and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness, joining cosmic provision to human experience.

column5: God as shepherd of Israel's flock
column6: The commentary places the shepherd and flock between guidance and pasture; the psalm calls God Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph like a flock, making national deliverance a pastoral relation.

column5: rain as a key held by God
column6: The commentary says rain descends in a measured amount and sustains pasture; the Talmud treats rain as a divine key, placing this ecological process among God's reserved acts and communal petitions.

column5: Pharaoh asks who the Lord is
column6: The commentary highlights Qur'anic Moses answering Pharaoh's “Who is your Lord?” with the Lord who gives each thing its form and guidance; Exodus has Pharaoh ask who YHWH is and refuse obedience, so the Qur'anic scene answers a biblical challenge with a positive account of creation and guidance.

column5: the chosen place of worship
column6: The commentary says a sacrificial animal is led until it reaches its appointed sanctuary; Deuteronomy tells Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and go there, supplying the Torah's destination for pilgrimage.

column5: offerings brought to the chosen place
column6: The commentary describes an animal whose journey ends at a sacred destination; Deuteronomy lists offerings Israel is to bring there, giving a specific ritual setting for destination-bound worship.

column5: God leads Israel through the wilderness for forty years
column6: The commentary says a measured path includes its duration and what the traveler learns along it; Moses recalls God leading Israel through the wilderness for forty years to humble and test them, making the journey's time purposeful.

column5: two spirits and two ways
column6: The commentary distinguishes God's act of guidance from the person's choice to follow or avoid the way; the Community Rule describes two spirits and their lots shaping opposing ways, making the tension between divine ordering and human conduct explicit in a sectarian frame.

column5: human cannot direct his own steps
column6: The commentary says a person cannot substitute private judgment for God's guidance; Jeremiah says a person's way is not in his own power and he cannot direct his steps, giving that limit a prayerful formulation.

column5: life as the Lord assigned and called
column6: The commentary says every being receives a measure and a way suited to it; Paul tells each person to live in the condition the Lord assigned and God called him to, applying that principle to vocation.

column5: star leads the travelers to the child
column6: The commentary says a celestial light may guide a traveler but is not itself the ultimate guide; Matthew's star goes before the Magi and stops over the child's place, treating the star as a sign that serves a destination.

column4: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 45
column5: shepherd, voice and faithful following
column6: The commentary reads the guide as one who goes ahead and whose followers choose to follow; Augustine's exposition of John 10 interprets the shepherd's voice and sheep as Christ's authority recognized by the faithful, turning pastoral leading into ecclesial interpretation.

column5: numbering days to gain wisdom
column6: The commentary says every thing has a measure and term; Moses asks God to teach people to number their days so they may gain a wise heart, turning the allotted lifespan into a discipline of judgment.

column5: days written before they begin
column6: The commentary says a creature's endpoint and lifespan belong to its measure; the psalm says the speaker's days were written before one of them existed, giving that claim a personal image of foreknown duration.
